title: John McCarthy
text:
John McCarthy was an American computer scientist and mathematician known for coining the term "artificial intelligence", which he selected to emphasize symbolic reasoning and distance the emerging field from cybernetics and automata theory, and founding the discipline through his organization of the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence.

He invented the Lisp programming language in 1958, which became the dominant language for AI research for decades due to its support for recursion, symbolic processing, and treating programs as data. McCarthy also pioneered concepts such as time-sharing systems in the late 1950s, enabling multiple users to interact with computers simultaneously, as well as foundational ideas in logical AI including the Advice Taker proposal for programs with common sense, the situation calculus for reasoning about actions and change, and circumscription as a form of non-monotonic reasoning.

Born in Boston, Massachusetts, on September 4, 1927, McCarthy earned a B.S. in mathematics from the California Institute of Technology in 1948 and a Ph.D. from Princeton University in 1951. His career included faculty positions at Dartmouth College, MIT, and Stanford University, where he founded and directed the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory starting in 1965 and remained until his retirement. He received numerous prestigious awards, including the ACM Turing Award in 1971 for his contributions to artificial intelligence, the Kyoto Prize in 1988, and the National Medal of Science in 1990. McCarthy died on October 24, 2011, in Stanford, California. His work profoundly shaped modern computing, from programming languages to knowledge representation and the philosophical foundations of intelligent systems.

#Early life

#Birth and family background

John McCarthy was born on September 4, 1927, in Boston, Massachusetts. His father, John Patrick McCarthy, was an Irish Catholic immigrant who worked as a carpenter, fisherman, and union organizer. His mother, Ida Glatt, was a Lithuanian Jewish immigrant who worked as a journalist and later as a social worker. Both parents were active in the Communist Party during the 1930s. The family moved from Boston to New York and eventually to Los Angeles. McCarthy had a younger brother named Patrick.

#Education and early development

McCarthy developed an early interest in science by reading popular science books. He attended Belmont High School in Los Angeles and graduated in 1943 after completing the program two years early. While in high school, he taught himself calculus from college-level textbooks. In 1944, he entered the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), skipping the first two years of mathematics courses, and earned his B.S. in mathematics in 1948. He then pursued graduate studies at Princeton University, receiving his Ph.D. in mathematics in 1951. During his time at Caltech, he attended the Hixon Symposium on Cerebral Mechanisms in Behavior in 1948, which sparked his interest in machine intelligence.

#Career

After earning his Ph.D. from Princeton University in 1951, John McCarthy began his academic career with short-term positions before focusing on artificial intelligence research. He served as acting assistant professor at Stanford University from 1953 to 1955.

He then moved to Dartmouth College, where he was an assistant professor from 1955 to 1958. During this period, he coined the term "artificial intelligence" in his August 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, which he organized and which took place in 1956; the event is widely regarded as the founding event of AI as an academic discipline. McCarthy later recalled that he had to choose a name for the proposal and selected "artificial intelligence". He distinguished his approach from that of Norbert Wiener's cybernetics, which emphasized direct feedback and numerical measures of error, while his own ideas focused on logical deduction from facts to achieve goals. He also expressed disappointment with earlier work on automata, noting that the papers submitted for the volume Automata Studies (published 1956), which he co-edited with Claude Shannon, were mostly about automata rather than intelligent behavior. In a 2011 oral history interview, McCarthy reflected that the term "machine intelligence", used by Donald Michie, might have been a better choice.

From 1958 to 1962, McCarthy was on the faculty at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), initially as an associate professor and later as a full professor. At MIT, he invented the Lisp programming language in 1958 and pioneered concepts in time-sharing operating systems in the late 1950s.

In 1962, he returned to Stanford University as a professor of computer science, where he spent the remainder of his career. He founded the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Project in 1963, which evolved into the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL) in 1965; he directed SAIL and remained actively involved in AI research there until his retirement. He became professor emeritus in 1994 but continued contributing to the field until his death in 2011.

#Personal life

#Family and relationships

John McCarthy was married three times. His first wife was Martha Coyote (also referred to as Martha White in some sources), and the marriage ended in divorce; they had two daughters, Susan McCarthy and Sarah McCarthy. His second wife was Vera Watson, a computer programmer and mountaineer, who died in 1978 in a climbing accident while attempting to scale Annapurna in the Himalayas. His third wife was Carolyn Talcott, with whom he had a son, Timothy Talcott McCarthy. McCarthy was survived by his third wife, his three children, and two grandchildren.

#Awards and honors

#Death

John McCarthy died on October 24, 2011, at his home in Stanford, California, at the age of 84.

#Legacy

McCarthy's legacy as the father of artificial intelligence endures through his foundational work in coining the term "artificial intelligence," developing the Lisp programming language, and advancing concepts in time-sharing, logical reasoning, and non-monotonic logic, profoundly influencing computer science and AI research for generations.
